name: Livermorium

discovery.discoverer: Joint Russian-American team, Dubna & Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive; observed only as individual atoms with sub-second half-lives.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, the American half of the joint team that created it alongside the Dubna laboratory in Russia.
ncertRelevance: named after a US national laboratory
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 16 below polonium, livermorium is expected to continue that group's trend toward more metallic character at the bottom, though so few atoms have ever been made that direct chemical confirmation remains extremely limited.
didYouKnow: Fewer than a hundred atoms of livermorium have likely ever been created across all experiments to date, each one detected purely by tracking its radioactive decay chain in the fraction of a second before it falls apart.
genZNote: Probably fewer than 100 atoms of this have ever existed, total, across all of human history. That's not a lot of livermorium to go around.
